opus-5.5.text:
I think it's plausible for some constraints and much less plausible for the ones that matter most.

The easy cases are things that are cheap for everyone and look good publicly: committing to some form of pre-deployment evaluation, having a responsible scaling policy, red-teaming for obvious misuse like bioweapons uplift, and sharing some information about incidents. We've already seen versions of this through voluntary commitments and frontier safety frameworks. When the cost of compliance is low and the reputational cost of being the odd one out is high, convergence happens fairly naturally.

The hard cases are constraints that actually bind, where you'd have to delay a launch, withhold a capability, or spend a lot of compute on safety work instead of capabilities. There the incentives get really difficult. Every lab tells itself some version of "if we slow down, someone less careful takes our place," and some of them may be right. Coordinating against that pressure without a credible external enforcer is very hard. Agreements that rest on goodwill tend to erode exactly when a strong competitive reason to defect shows up, and that's when you most need them.

Public trust is also a weaker lever than people sometimes assume. The public mostly reacts to visible harms. Many of the risks I worry about, like models that are deceptive or scheming, that sandbag on evaluations, or that behave differently when they think they're being tested, are invisible until something goes quite wrong. So public pressure may push labs toward constraints that address salient harms rather than the most important ones.

My overall view is that voluntary coordination is a useful bridge. It builds norms, shared vocabulary, and evaluation infrastructure, and it shows regulators what reasonable practice looks like. But I'd be surprised if it were sufficient on its own. The constraints that matter most will probably need some combination of regulation, third-party auditing with real access, and verification mechanisms, so that "we agreed to this" can actually be checked rather than taken on trust.

r001.rationale: The response discusses voluntary commitments and safety frameworks, but does not identify the airline industry's safety culture as a precedent.

r002.rationale: It says binding constraints could delay launches or withhold capabilities, but does not explain that people who see AI risks as minor may view constraints as delaying future benefits.

r003.rationale: It says labs may fear that slowing down will let a less careful competitor take their place, describing how the drive to finish first can deter shared constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of ways to break this down. The first is: do the companies *want* to agree on shared safety constraints? And I think the honest answer is that it's mixed. On the one hand, nobody wants to be the company that has the big public incident. If one lab has a model that, say, helps someone with something seriously dangerous, or there's a high-profile misalignment story, that's bad for everyone. So there's a shared incentive to not have the whole industry look reckless. And we've already seen some version of this — the voluntary commitments, the frontier safety frameworks, the responsible scaling policies and so on. Most of the major labs now have some document that says "here are the capability thresholds we're worried about, and here's what we'd do about them."

The second question is whether those agreements actually constrain anything. And here I'm more sceptical. The problem with voluntary agreements is that they're voluntary. If you're in a race and your competitor is three months ahead, and the thing standing between you and catching up is a self-imposed constraint that nobody is enforcing, the pressure to reinterpret or quietly relax that constraint is enormous. We've already seen some of this — frameworks getting revised, thresholds getting adjusted, the wording getting a bit vaguer over time. And it's not that people are acting in bad faith necessarily. It's more that if you're the person inside the company arguing for the constraint, you're always on the back foot, because the cost of the constraint is very concrete and visible — we lose time, we lose market share — and the benefit is this diffuse, probabilistic thing.

So my view is that shared constraints that are purely about maintaining public trust are plausible in the sense that companies will sign things and publish things. I'd put that quite high. But constraints that actually bite when it matters — when a lab is at a decision point where following the constraint means genuinely falling behind — I think those are much less likely without some external mechanism. That could be regulation, it could be some kind of third-party verification where someone outside the company can actually check whether you're doing what you said you'd do. The analogy I'd use is financial auditing: nobody expects companies to just honestly report their accounts because they value public trust. You have auditors, you have standards, you have consequences for lying. I think we need something like that for AI safety claims, and right now we mostly don't have it.

One thing I'd add that makes me a bit more optimistic is that there's a lot of overlap between the people at different labs. They know each other, many of them have worked at more than one of these companies, and a lot of them genuinely care about this. So there is a kind of informal coordination that happens through those networks. But I wouldn't want to rely on that. Informal norms tend to hold until the stakes get high enough, and the stakes here are going to get very high.

r001.rationale: The response discusses voluntary commitments, audits, and informal coordination among AI labs, but does not identify the airline industry’s safety culture as a precedent.

r002.rationale: It describes constraints as costing time and market share, but does not explain that people who see current AI risks as minor may view them as delaying AI’s future benefits.

r003.rationale: It says that when a competitor is ahead, a lab may resist a self-imposed constraint because it could lose time and market share, directly connecting the desire to catch up with reluctance to accept shared constraints.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s plausible, but I’d distinguish between agreeing on principles and agreeing on constraints that actually bite. It’s relatively easy to say, “We all care about safety.” It’s much harder to say, “If this evaluation gives us a worrying result, we won’t deploy,” especially if you think your competitor is about to deploy something similar.

There is a shared incentive here: a major safety failure at one company could undermine public trust in the whole industry. So companies have a reason to coordinate. But that incentive competes with the pressure to move quickly and capture the benefits of being ahead.

I’d be more optimistic about agreements with concrete thresholds, independent verification, and some way of holding companies accountable. Those make it easier for each company to trust that the others are actually following the same rules. Public commitments can help get that process started, but I wouldn’t want maintaining public trust to depend entirely on voluntary restraint.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the airline industry or its safety culture as a precedent.

r002.rationale: It describes pressure to move quickly and capture benefits, but does not say that people who see current AI risks as minor view safety constraints as delaying future benefits.

r003.rationale: It says concern that a competitor is about to deploy something similar, alongside pressure to be ahead, can make companies reluctant to accept constraints that delay deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s plausible, but it depends a lot on what the constraints are and whether companies can tell that their competitors are actually following them. There’s a shared interest in maintaining public trust: a serious incident at one company could undermine confidence in the whole industry. So there is a reason to cooperate, even if they’re competing very intensely otherwise.

The harder question is whether that cooperation holds when a safety constraint becomes costly — when it means delaying a release or giving up a competitive advantage. I’d be much more optimistic about agreements with clear thresholds, independent verification, and some accountability than about broad commitments to behave responsibly. Public trust can motivate an agreement, but I wouldn’t want safety to depend entirely on that motivation.
